doc.title: Tom Varner interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 13, 2025

title: Listening widely in the mid-70s: straight-ahead to avant garde
summary: Varner learned form by listening; his generation heard Ornette, Brown, Parker, Braxton and Mitchell together and mixed approaches by 19.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Did you get the – early on the idea of, I’ll call it the typical jazz performance where the head is at the beginning and at the end. And in the middle there’s this as long as it goes. But still with structure. Did that dawn on you by yourself or did you have help from a teacher?

Good question. Well I was just listening and listening and listening so much that – but what was unique perhaps for me or my age, those kids that were like in high school in the mid-‘70s. I was high school class of ’75. We were listening – we weren’t doing that thing of like you can’t walk until you learn to crawl. A lot of us were listening to Ornette Coleman and Clifford Brown and Charlie Parker and very quickly and Anthony Braxton and Roscoe Mitchell and – so music that would be considered more quote straight ahead jazz and music that was considered quote avant garde jazz and music that was perhaps more structurally post-modern and music that was, like you said, theme, solo-solo-solo, trade, trade fours with the drums, theme, and out. So by the time I was maybe 19 I was already doing a mix of those different approaches.
